name: Harris Chain of Lakes
type: Chain of lakes linked by canals and creeks: grass, pads, shell bars and fish attractors
pool: Regulated by locks;Levels change little through the year
notes: Coolest water. Bass stage near the spawning flats; specks school offshore.
Spawn starts on warm spells. Big bass move shallow around the moon.
Peak spawn for bass and specks around the full moon.
Post-spawn. Shellcracker spawn on the full moon.
Shad spawn at dawn; bluegill bed on the full moon.
Summer pattern: topwater early, then mats and offshore grass.
Hottest stretch. Fish first light, last light and after storms.
Hottest water. Short bites at dawn and around storms.
Shad move shallow as the nights cool.
Fall feed. Bass school on shad in creeks and canals.
Cold fronts start the speck bite offshore.
Cold fronts. Bass on outside grass; specks school in open water.

flbass.doing: Cold water pulls bass to deep channel swings and main-lake holes, like the lagoon off Leesburg. The best bite is often the warm middle of the day.
how: Wild shiners on channel swings and in the holes.
Slow-swimming plastics or a vertical jig over fish you mark.
Midday warmth, especially on the second or third warm day.

specks.doing: Specks school in open water over the deepest flats, channels and offshore grass, suspended at a different depth from day to day.
how: Missouri minnows or grass shrimp, or spider-rig small jigs (hair jigs, tubes, Hal Flies).
Set minnows at several depths, then match the one that bites.
Cast a small jig to schools you see on forward-facing sonar.

bream.doing: Slow. Bluegill and shellcracker hold in deeper grass, canals and around docks; warm, sunny afternoons bring them up.
how: Grass shrimp on the bottom next to hydrilla or eelgrass.
Small jig or worm along canal edges and docks.

flbass.doing: Late January into early February, bass stage near Haines Creek and the Dead River, on main-lake points, in the canals and on eelgrass as the water climbs into the upper 50s.
how: Crankbait or vibrating jig along the staging edges.
Plastics flipped into the first cover off the flats.

specks.doing: Schools leave the open water for pad fields, bulrush and Kissimmee grass that sit next to deeper water. A cold front pushes them back out.
how: Troll or drift minnow-tipped jigs along the outside of the pads and reeds.
Minnow under a cork in openings at the grass edge.
Fish the closest open water off the same grass.

bream.doing: Shellcracker move onto firm sand and shell near the grass ahead of the spring full moons; bluegill feed around reeds and docks.
how: Red wigglers on the bottom with a split shot.
Crickets or grass shrimp under a small float along reeds.

flbass.doing: Mid-February through March, bass spawn in hard-bottom canals, along reed lines and on isolated eelgrass, especially on Lake Dora, the Dead River and the canal networks.
how: Senko, soft lizard or flipping bait in junebug or black and blue.
Big fish often come around the full and new moons.

specks.doing: Around the moon phases, specks move shallow to spawn on pad groups, Kissimmee grass edges and openings in the vegetation. Between moons they sit in the closest deeper water.
how: Jig or live bait in the openings; once you catch one, others are close.
Fish the nearest deep water and change bait depth until they bite.

bream.doing: Shellcracker bed on the March and April full moons on firm sand and shell near grass. Bluegill start as the water warms.
how: Red wigglers on the bottom; work the area until you find the colony.
Small beetle spin along the edge of the flat.

flbass.doing: From late March, bass leave the beds for the nearest drop-off and mid-depth grass. The April and May full moons put bluegill on sand and eelgrass flats, and bass follow.
how: Swim jig, vibrating jig or a steady swimbait along the first drop.
Frog, popper or dark plastic early and late.

specks.doing: After the spawn, specks scatter to deeper grass edges, docks, bridges and channel edges. The bite slows as the water warms.
how: Minnows at dock pilings, bridges and fish attractors.
Small jig swum along the deep edge of the vegetation.

bream.doing: The April and May full moons put bluegill on beds on sand and eelgrass flats, and shellcracker in tight canals and creek mouths.
how: Crickets under a cork over the flats.
Red wigglers on the bottom in canals and creek mouths.

flbass.doing: Pads, docks and fresh grass from first light to about 8 a.m. By July, bass move offshore to Haines Creek, Helena Run and main-lake shell bars, humps and drops in 8 to 20 ft.
how: Buzzbait, frog or walking bait, then a crankbait or slow-rolled plastic.
Deep crankbait, heavy jig or big worm in green pumpkin or plum.
Spinnerbait or vibrating jig at feeder creeks and wind-blown points right after rain.

specks.doing: The slowest season. Specks suspend in the deepest water, on fish attractors and in shade; fish early, late or at night.
how: Lights and minnows at bridges and deep docks.
Vertical jig or minnow at the depth you mark.

bream.doing: Bluegill keep spawning on each full moon; between moons they hold in deeper pads, grass patches and around docks. Fish early.
how: Grass shrimp in deep pads and hydrilla patches; anchor and chum lightly.
Worms and crickets along the walkways.

flbass.doing: Bass leave the offshore spots for the flats and follow shad to wind-blown points, creek mouths and canals. Moving water in the Dora Canal, Dead River and Haines Creek, along heavy hydrilla edges, is key.
how: Alabama rig, jerkbait or a big spinnerbait; frog or popper when shad ball up.
Lipless crankbait, swimbait or vibrating jig along hydrilla edges in moving water.
Squarebill or swim jig in the Lake Griffin canals.

specks.doing: The bite stays slow until the first good cold fronts. Then Lake Harris, Griffin, Eustis, Dora and little Lake Carlton all produce, in open water near drop-offs and around fish attractors.
how: Open water near drop-offs at several depths.
Vertical jig or troll over them, keeping lines high enough to avoid snags.
Bright jigs tipped with a minnow, or a plain minnow.

bream.doing: Bream feed hard in the grass as the water cools. Fewer beds, steady numbers.
how: Anchor near a thick hydrilla patch and fish grass shrimp or worms near the bottom.
Crickets under a cork along reed lines.
